subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on sociological theories of crime and deviance, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain sociological theories of crime and deviance for GCSE Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Definitions of crime and deviance and their social construction
Functionalist theory and Merton's strain theory
Marxist and subcultural theories of crime
Measuring crime: official statistics, victim and self-report surveys, the dark figure
Patterns of crime by class, age, gender and ethnicity

questions.lo: Definitions of crime and deviance and their social construction
questions.q: What is the difference between 'crime' and 'deviance'?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
Crime is behaviour that breaks the law; deviance is behaviour that breaks social norms but may not be illegal
Crime applies only to adults; deviance only to children
Deviance is always illegal; crime is never illegal
questions.explain: Crime is behaviour that breaks the law and is punishable by the state. Deviance is behaviour that breaks society's norms; it may or may not be illegal (e.g. talking loudly in a library is deviant but not criminal).

questions.lo: Definitions of crime and deviance and their social construction
questions.q: The fact that an act (e.g. drinking alcohol) may be legal in one society but illegal in another shows that crime and deviance are:
options: Always defined the same way everywhere
Socially constructed and relative to time, place and culture
questions.explain: Crime and deviance are socially constructed: what counts as deviant varies between societies, cultures and historical periods, so they are relative rather than fixed or natural categories.

questions.lo: Formal and informal social control
questions.q: Which of the following is an agency of FORMAL social control?
questions.explain: Formal social control is carried out by official agencies with written rules and sanctions, such as the police, courts and prisons. The family, peer group and religion are agencies of informal social control.

questions.lo: Formal and informal social control
questions.q: A teenager avoids swearing at home because they fear their parents' disapproval. This is an example of:
options: Informal social control through the family
questions.explain: Informal social control uses unwritten rules and sanctions such as disapproval, praise or ridicule. Here the family exerts control through the fear of parental disapproval.

questions.lo: Functionalist theory and Merton's strain theory
questions.q: Functionalists such as Durkheim argue that a certain amount of crime is:
options: Inevitable and can even perform positive functions for society
Caused only by the ruling class
questions.explain: Durkheim argued crime is inevitable and even functional: it can reinforce shared values (boundary maintenance), allow social change and act as a safety valve, so some crime is normal in every society.

questions.lo: Functionalist theory and Merton's strain theory
questions.q: Merton's strain theory explains crime as resulting from a gap between:
options: Society's shared goals (such as wealth) and the legitimate means available to achieve them
questions.explain: Merton argued that when people accept society's goals (e.g. material success) but lack legitimate means to reach them, the resulting 'strain' can push some to 'innovate' and turn to crime.

questions.lo: Functionalist theory and Merton's strain theory
questions.q: According to Merton, a person who accepts the goal of wealth but uses illegal means such as theft to achieve it is an example of a(n):
questions.explain: Merton called this response 'innovation': the person accepts the cultural goal (success/wealth) but rejects the legitimate means, using illegitimate means such as crime to achieve it.

questions.lo: Labelling theory and Becker
questions.q: Howard Becker's labelling theory argues that an act becomes deviant when:
options: Others successfully apply the label 'deviant' to it and to the person
It is committed by a working-class person
It is naturally and universally wrong
questions.explain: Becker argued that no act is inherently deviant; deviance is created when society labels an act and a person as deviant. Deviance is the result of the reaction of others, not the act itself.

questions.lo: Labelling theory and Becker
questions.q: In labelling theory, a 'master status' is:
options: A label (such as 'criminal') that overrides all other aspects of a person's identity
The highest rank in the police force
questions.explain: Once someone is labelled deviant, 'criminal' can become their master status, the main way others see them. This can trap them in a deviant career and produce further (secondary) deviance.

questions.lo: Labelling theory and Becker
questions.q: A young man is labelled a 'criminal' after one offence, finds it hard to get work, and commits further crime. Labelling theorists call this later offending:
questions.explain: Secondary deviance is deviance that follows from being labelled. The reaction to the original (primary) act pushes the person into a deviant role, leading to further offending.

questions.lo: Marxist and subcultural theories of crime
questions.q: Marxist theories argue that the law and the criminal justice system tend to:
options: Serve the interests of the ruling class while focusing on the crimes of the working class
questions.explain: Marxists argue that law-making and enforcement protect ruling-class interests. Powerful groups' crimes (e.g. corporate crime) are under-policed, while working-class 'street' crime is heavily targeted.

questions.lo: Marxist and subcultural theories of crime
questions.q: Albert Cohen's subcultural theory explains delinquency as arising from 'status frustration'. This means that:
options: Deviance is caused only by labelling
All crime is committed for financial gain
Working-class boys who fail to gain status legitimately gain it by breaking norms within a subculture
questions.explain: Cohen argued that working-class boys denied status in mainstream society (e.g. at school) experience status frustration. They form delinquent subcultures where they gain status by inverting mainstream values.

questions.lo: Marxist and subcultural theories of crime
questions.q: Which of these is a key criticism of subcultural theories of crime?
options: They ignore the existence of groups altogether
They tend to over-predict working-class delinquency and largely ignore female and middle-class crime
questions.explain: Subcultural theories focus mainly on working-class male delinquency, so critics argue they neglect female offending, middle-class and white-collar crime, and assume everyone shares the same mainstream goals.

questions.lo: Measuring crime: official statistics, victim and self-report surveys, the dark figure
questions.q: The 'dark figure of crime' refers to:
options: Crime that is unreported and/or unrecorded, so it does not appear in official statistics
questions.explain: The dark figure of crime is the gap between crime that actually happens and crime recorded in official statistics, made up of offences that are never reported to or recorded by the police.

questions.lo: Measuring crime: official statistics, victim and self-report surveys, the dark figure
questions.q: A 'victim survey', such as the Crime Survey for England and Wales, measures crime by:
options: Asking offenders which crimes they have committed
Asking members of the public about crimes they have experienced, including unreported ones
Counting only crimes recorded by the police
questions.explain: Victim surveys ask people about their experiences of crime, whether or not they reported it. This helps reveal some of the dark figure that official statistics miss.

questions.lo: Measuring crime: official statistics, victim and self-report surveys, the dark figure
questions.q: A researcher gives people an anonymous questionnaire asking which offences they themselves have committed. This method is a:
questions.explain: A self-report study asks respondents to admit (usually anonymously) to crimes they have committed. It can uncover hidden offending but may suffer from exaggeration, concealment or memory problems.

questions.lo: Patterns of crime by class, age, gender and ethnicity
questions.q: Official statistics consistently suggest that recorded crime is committed most by:
questions.explain: Official statistics show that recorded offenders are disproportionately young and male. Sociologists debate how far this reflects real behaviour and how far it reflects policing, labelling and reporting.

questions.lo: Patterns of crime by class, age, gender and ethnicity
questions.q: The 'chivalry thesis' is one explanation for why women appear less often in crime statistics. It argues that:
options: The (mostly male) criminal justice system treats women more leniently, so their offending is under-recorded
Women are always given the harshest sentences
questions.explain: The chivalry thesis suggests the criminal justice system treats women more leniently, so female crime may be under-reported and under-recorded, partly explaining the gender gap in the statistics.

questions.lo: The media and crime
questions.q: Sociologists argue that the media often give a distorted picture of crime by:
options: Over-representing violent and unusual crimes, which are actually less common
Reporting crime in exact proportion to how often it occurs
questions.explain: The media over-report dramatic, violent and unusual crimes because they make good stories, even though such crimes are relatively rare. This gives a distorted picture and can increase fear of crime.

questions.lo: The media and crime
questions.q: Exaggerated media coverage that presents a group as 'folk devils' and creates public alarm out of proportion to the real threat is known as a:
questions.explain: A moral panic (Stanley Cohen) is an exaggerated media-driven reaction to a group seen as a threat (folk devils). It can amplify deviance and shape public and police responses to crime.
